body.text: The main purpose of insurgencies is to deadlock the conflict on the battlefield through guerrilla warfare to open up space for political dialogue with a conventionally superior adversary. However, if insurgents avoid negotiations (for any tactical or strategic reason), the asymmetric battlefield advantage eventually dissipates, resulting in further militarization of the conflict and alienation, at some level, of the rank-and-file from the top leadership.

In this regard, the recent leadership transition in the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA)-Jeeyand from Bashir Zaib to Rahman Gul, differences between BLA-Azad’s field commanders and its leader Hyrbyair Marri, and BLA-Azad’s differences with the Baloch Liberation Front (BLF) are instructive.

Baloch insurgent groups were once riven with factionalism, leadership disputes over allegations of financial misappropriation, and turf wars. Between 2018 and 2025, those frictions subsided. This paved the way for coalition building, organizational consolidation and consistency in the leadership’s decision-making and military strategy, and institutionalization of specialized units.

After eight years, the old wounds of the Baloch insurgency have opened up again. The decision of the Baloch insurgent leadership, especially former BLA-Jeeyand chief Bashir Zaib and BLF head Dr. Allah Nazar Baloch, to avoid political dialogue appears to have pushed the Baloch insurgency back to the factionalism and disputes of the past.

In November, BLA-Jeeyand deposed Zaib as its chief following a decision of the Senior Command Council. It subsequently appointed Rahman Gul, who is also head of the Majeed Brigade, as Zaib’s successor. The BLA-Jeeyand’s official statement framed Zaib’s removal as a consensus decision and part of the organization’s constitutional democratic process to avoid the formation of personality cults and hereditary leadership.

Today, BLA-Jeeyand’s official statements are silent on Zaib. Unlike Aslam, the founder of BLA-Jeeyand, who is showered with praise and love, there isn’t a word of appreciation for Zaib’s services and contributions to the Baloch insurgency. Under his command, BLA-Jeeyand emerged as South Asia’s most potent and disciplined insurgency. BLA-Jeeyand owes a lot to Zaib for what it is and where it is today. Likewise, official releases have not provided any hint or clarity about Zaib’s future status and role within BLA-Jeeyand. This indicates that all is not well within the insurgent group. Zaib is an icon of the contemporary Baloch insurgency and a larger-than-life figure for many Baloch separatists. His quiet departure from the scene points to brewing trouble within the group.

Two rumors provide clues to what could have led to Zaib’s ouster and Gul’s appointment. The first is that Bashir has serious health issues and may no longer be able to lead the group, while the other points to serious differences between Zaib and Gul following the disastrous outcome of Operation Herof 2.0.

Unlike Herof 1.0, which BLA-Jeeyand launched near-simultaneously in 13 districts of Balochistan, Herof 2.0 was a damp squib. It flouted the cardinal principle of insurgency of focusing on mobile hit-and-run operations. Herof 2.0 involved large concentrations of BLA fighters in several places, making it easier for Pakistani security forces to spot and surveil their retreating positions, and subsequently hunt them down in Operation Rad-ul-Fitna 2.0.

The Pakistan Army claimed to have killed as many as 216 fighters of BLA-Jeeyand in Rad-ul-Fitna 2.0, while the group has acknowledged the loss of only 93 fighters. These losses dealt a blow to the group especially since it gained nothing substantive from the offensive. It raised serious questions about Zaib’s operational strategies. Consequently, Zaib was allegedly sidelined from decision-making in February, and Gul managed BLA-Jeeyand’s administrative, military, and institutional matters with the help of the Senior Command Council.

During this period, Zaib did not issue any statements; his last video message was before the launch of Herof 2.0. Neither has Hakkal Media, which has been publishing various books authored by Zaib, published any statements issued by the former BLA-Jeeyand chief.

It remains to be seen whether the Senior Command Council’s decision to remove Zaib will be accepted by his loyalists or whether they will rise in revolt, as Aslam and Zaib did against BLA-Azad’s decision to depose them in 2016.

Leadership transitions in Baloch insurgent groups have always been contentious and bloody. Although Zaib’s removal was not accompanied by bloodshed, it was not the result of a consultative process; rather, it is a byproduct of brewing internal differences over operational strategies, leadership style, and institutional policies.

Concurrently, trouble has been brewing in BLA-Azad since April 2026, when several commanders demanded accountability and the introduction of an organizational constitution from its leader, Hyrbyair Marri. However, Marri’s dilatory tactics resulted in the formation of a Reformed Command Council, which deposed the top leaders until the implementation of required reforms. The Reformed Command Council has also alleged that Marri and his loyalists committed financial misappropriation. It remains to be seen whether BLA-Azad and the Reformed Command Council manage to resolve their differences or part ways.

At the same time, a public war of words has erupted between BLA-Azad and BLF over the Dasht-e-Goran operation, where BLA-Azad attacked the house of Baloch tribal elder Qambar Khan Mengal on October 15. Allegedly, BLA-Azad used the BLF’s flags during a ten-hour operation against Qambar Khan. On October 17, BLF spokesperson Major Gwahram Baloch formally distanced his organization from the attack and accused BLA-Azad of using the former’s flag. He questioned BLA-Azad’s organizational discipline and right to act in the name of Baloch separatism.

Taken together, these are extraordinary developments inconsistent with trends observed in the Baloch insurgency’s landscape since 2018. The fissures and cleavages emerging today were last seen during the 2010-2017 period. Since then, tribal influence on the Baloch insurgency has declined visibly as its center of gravity has shifted to the educated middle class. Also, mergers, unifications and coalitions replaced tribal rivalries, organizational turf wars, and leadership disputes.
These developments have significant consequences for the insurgency and the counterinsurgency operations in Balochistan.

With regard to the insurgent landscape, it remains to be seen whether the Gul and Zaib factions as well as Hyrbyair Marri and the Reformed Command Council, manage to reconcile their differences or not. If these differences, which seem intractable, widen further, the rebel factions of Zaib and the BLA-Azad’s Reformed Command Council could form separate groups, which would take the total number of BLA groups to four.

If they merge to form one group, the BLA would have three factions. It is also possible that elements of the Reformed Command Council might join the BLA-Jeeyand or the BLF. Irrespective of the outcomes, the old wounds of Baloch insurgency have been reopened.

On the counterinsurgency side, Pakistani security institutions could exploit these divisions. Several restless Baloch insurgent commanders and fighters, who are unsure of their future, could turn informers for the state in return for indemnity or concessions on their sentences. State institutions can also use intermediaries to offer reconciliation to factions willing to disarm and come within the Pakistani constitutional framework.
Finally, no one has seen Gul and Zaib for the last several months. The Baloch insurgent fighters and commanders deserve to know whether these individuals are alive or not.

The Baloch insurgency has thrown away its tactical battlefield advantage by choosing to further militarize the conflict. After years of enjoying a tactical upper hand vis-à-vis the security forces, the battlefield pendulum is shifting in favor of the Pakistani state. However, the conflict will persist, and any respite for the Pakistani state from these changes will be tactical and temporary because the structural factors of this conflict, which are political and have no security solution, remain unresolved.
